text: Lessons 17 and 18 covered what belongs in lineage documentation and how to draw it as a diagram. This lesson covers how that documentation actually gets built and kept current in the first place — written by hand, generated by a tool scanning real pipeline code, or, in practice, usually some hybrid of both.

Manual lineage is documentation someone writes by hand — a diagram drawn in a tool, a wiki page, a spreadsheet of source-to-target mappings. It's the fastest way to start: no tooling investment, just someone who understands the pipeline writing down what they know. The weakness is durability — it's accurate the day it's drawn, and every schema change or new pipeline after that requires someone to remember to update it, which deadline pressure makes the first thing skipped.

Automated lineage is generated by a tool that scans actual pipeline code, SQL queries, or execution logs, building the graph from what the code actually does rather than what someone remembers. A tool parsing SELECT and JOIN clauses can infer that FactTable depends on StagingView without a human ever typing that relationship in. This stays current almost by definition — re-run the scan after a change, and the graph updates with it, at the cost of real tooling investment.

The real trade-off is what automated scanning can't see: a manual Excel export emailed to a stakeholder, a one-off script run from someone's laptop, a copy-paste into another system — none of that shows up, because none of it is code a tool can parse. Those undocumented, manual hops are often exactly where the most dangerous gaps live, precisely because nothing is watching them. Most mature practices end up hybrid: automation as the backbone, manual documentation filling the rest.

Next lesson: lineage tools overview — the real, named tools organizations actually use to automate this, what category each one falls into, from enterprise catalogs to open-source frameworks, and where an open standard like OpenLineage fits in alongside them.
